paragraphs: This paper examines the practical work of making machine learning datasets fairer. Its starting point is that substantial effort has gone into this goal, while the realities of dataset curation remain less well understood. The researchers approach that gap by interviewing 30 dataset curators, grounding their study in the experiences of people who carry out this work.

The main contribution is a taxonomy: an organized account of challenges and trade-offs across the dataset curation lifecycle. Looking across the lifecycle matters because it frames fairness as something shaped throughout the work of building a dataset. The emphasis on trade-offs also directs attention to competing considerations that curators encounter when making decisions.

The findings connect these practical difficulties to broader issues in the fairness landscape. On that basis, the paper offers recommendations for systemic changes that could better support fair dataset curation. Its contribution is an interview-based understanding of the problem and an organizational framework for discussing it, with recommendations directed beyond individual curation decisions.
neurips-2024-a-taxonomy-of-challenges-to.tldr: Interviews with 30 dataset curators inform a taxonomy of fairness challenges and recommendations for systemic change.

paragraphs: Image interpolation aims to produce transitions between images or generation conditions. For text-conditioned or image-conditioned diffusion models, simply blending the conditions can produce inconsistent images with poor fidelity. This paper introduces Attention Interpolation via Diffusion, or AID, as a training-free way to improve those transitions.

AID changes how interpolation happens within attention. It combines inner and outer attention interpolation in a fused layer designed to improve consistency and fidelity. It also selects interpolation coefficients through a beta distribution to improve smoothness. These contributions address both the mechanism that combines information and the choice of intermediate positions along the transition.

The authors also introduce PAID, a prompt-guided variant that treats interpolation as generation dependent on a condition. Experiments report improvements in consistency, smoothness, and efficiency, with results closely aligned with human preferences. PAID additionally shows benefits for combining concepts, controlled editing, image morphing, and image-controlled generation. Both variants remain training-free, making attention manipulation the central means of controlling the generated transitions.
neurips-2024-aid-attention-interpolation.tldr: AID improves diffusion-image transitions without training by interpolating attention and choosing coefficients to promote smoother changes.

paragraphs: Automatic prompt optimization helps turn user input into prompts that produce good images. Many methods assume the image generator remains fixed, raising a problem when prompts must work with a previously unseen generator. This paper formalizes that challenge as model-generalized automatic prompt optimization: training with known models and testing generalization to unseen ones.

AP-Adapter tackles the task in two stages. First, a language model rewrites the prompts. Second, the method builds an enhanced representation space using differences between image-generation models. It stores characteristics of multiple models as domain prototypes, which act as reference points for adjusting prompt representations. Those adjusted representations then produce conditioning information for controllable image generation.

The authors curate a dataset containing multiple diffusion models and their associated text-image data. Their experiments confirm that existing prompt optimizers perform suboptimally on unseen models and demonstrate that AP-Adapter can generalize prompts well in this setting while producing high-quality images. The contribution makes differences between generators part of the optimization process, rather than leaving transfer to unseen generators unaddressed.
neurips-2024-ap-adapter-improving-genera.tldr: AP-Adapter uses prompt rewriting and representations of model differences to improve automatic prompts on unseen diffusion generators.

paragraphs: Attribution maps explain a vision model's prediction by assigning importance scores to input features. Evaluating whether these scores provide good explanations is difficult. This paper targets two weaknesses in a widely used evaluation procedure that progressively deletes input information: it can move inputs outside the model's usual domain, and it does not support comparisons between models.

The authors introduce an evaluation protocol that overcomes these two limitations. They use it to assess 23 attribution methods and to examine how design choices in popular vision networks affect attribution quality. This extends the evaluation question from which explanation method works well to how the network being explained influences the result.

Under the proposed evaluation, intrinsically explainable models outperform standard models. Raw attribution values also show higher quality than earlier work had indicated. Changes to network design produce consistent changes in attribution quality, with some standard design choices helping. Together, these findings show why the evaluation protocol, attribution method, and underlying model all matter when judging visual explanations.
neurips-2024-benchmarking-the-attributio.tldr: A new attribution-evaluation protocol supports comparisons across vision models and reveals how model design affects explanation quality.

paragraphs: Graph Transformers have become popular for assigning labels to nodes in graphs, supported by theoretical expressiveness and strong benchmark results. This paper revisits their reported advantage over traditional message-passing graph neural networks. It asks whether the comparisons gave established models sufficiently effective hyperparameter settings.

The authors reevaluate three classic architectures: GCN, GAT, and GraphSAGE. With slight hyperparameter tuning, these models achieve state-of-the-art performance, matching or exceeding recent Graph Transformers on 17 of the 18 datasets examined. The result suggests that some previously reported superiority of Graph Transformers may reflect suboptimal baseline configurations.

The study also uses ablations to investigate normalization, dropout, residual connections, and network depth. These analyses examine how configuration choices contribute to node-classification performance. The broader implication is methodological: architecture comparisons need strong, appropriately configured baselines to support conclusions about model capabilities. The reported results establish the competitiveness of classic GNNs across the evaluated datasets without turning that empirical finding into a universal ranking of graph architectures.
neurips-2024-classic-gnns-are-strong-bas.tldr: Slightly tuned classic GNNs match or exceed recent Graph Transformers on 17 of 18 examined node-classification datasets.

paragraphs: Choosing pretraining data shapes a language model's later performance, but identifying an optimal subset is generally considered intractable. CoLoR-Filter provides a computationally efficient selection heuristic for targeted pretraining. Its criterion comes from an empirical Bayes-inspired approach and uses the relative losses assigned by two auxiliary models.

The authors evaluate selection from C4 for two purposes: adapting to Books and improving a suite of multiple-choice question-answering tasks. They report favorable scaling as selection becomes more aggressive and when small auxiliary models select data for larger target models. This makes the cost of the selectors an important part of the approach's practicality.

In a headline comparison, two auxiliary models with 150 million parameters select data for a 1.2-billion-parameter model. The resulting model matches a same-sized model trained on 25 billion randomly selected tokens while using 25 times less data for Books and 11 times less for the downstream tasks. These results demonstrate substantial data savings in the evaluated settings, supporting targeted selection as a way to improve pretraining efficiency.
neurips-2024-color-filter-conditional-lo.tldr: CoLoR-Filter uses two small models' relative losses to select pretraining data that achieves comparable performance with substantially fewer tokens.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation transfers capabilities from a larger teacher language model to a smaller student, helping address computational and storage demands. This paper focuses on a mismatch in how distillation effort is distributed across domains. A student may already be close to its teacher in some domains while remaining much further behind in others.

The authors argue that existing approaches overlook these differences, devoting too much attention to domains with small performance gaps and too little to domains with large gaps. Their framework, DDK, changes the composition of the distillation dataset dynamically according to the teacher-student performance differences. It makes these adjustments smoothly to support a more stable and effective learning process.

Extensive evaluations report significant improvements in student performance, with DDK outperforming both continuously pretrained baselines and existing distillation methods by a large margin. The findings support adapting the training-data mixture to where the student needs more knowledge. The main contribution is therefore a domain-sensitive allocation of distillation data as learning proceeds.
neurips-2024-ddk-distilling-domain-knowl.tldr: DDK improves language-model distillation by smoothly adjusting domain data mixtures according to teacher-student performance gaps.

paragraphs: Curriculum reinforcement learning helps an agent learn through a sequence of increasingly complex tasks. Choosing that sequence can be difficult without knowledge of the environment. DiCuRL addresses this problem by using a conditional diffusion model to generate goals that challenge the agent while remaining achievable.

The method incorporates both a Q-function and a trainable reward function based on Adversarial Intrinsic Motivation into the diffusion model. These provide information for estimating how close the agent is to achieving a goal. The diffusion model's noising and denoising process also promotes exploration. Together, these components connect goal generation to the agent's progress while supporting the search for new learning opportunities.

The authors describe DiCuRL as environment-agnostic and able to construct curricula without relying on domain knowledge. They evaluate it in three maze environments and two robotic manipulation tasks simulated in MuJoCo. Across these evaluations, it outperforms or matches nine state-of-the-art curriculum-learning algorithms. The results support diffusion-based goal generation as an effective curriculum mechanism in the tested environments.
neurips-2024-diffusion-based-curriculum-.tldr: DiCuRL uses conditional diffusion to generate achievable but challenging goals and matches or outperforms nine curriculum-learning methods in evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: This paper asks how language models internally represent a world described in text, including entities and their relationships. Instead of checking only whether a complete world state can be recovered, it examines whether models retain useful abstractions. Such abstractions may preserve information needed for a task without representing every aspect of the world equally.

The proposed framework draws on state abstraction theory from reinforcement learning. It distinguishes general abstractions that support prediction of future states from goal-oriented abstractions that support actions toward a task's objective. To investigate this distinction, the authors design a text-based planning task in which a language-model agent interacts with objects in containers to reach a specified goal state.

The experiments find that fine-tuning and advanced pretraining strengthen a tendency to maintain goal-oriented abstractions during decoding. Representations increasingly favor task completion over recovery of the world's full state and dynamics. This finding changes how probing results can be interpreted: the relevant question includes what an internal representation supports, alongside how completely it describes the environment.
neurips-2024-do-llms-build-world-represe.tldr: A state-abstraction probing framework finds that fine-tuning and advanced pretraining strengthen goal-oriented world representations in a text-based planning task.

paragraphs: The paper studies repeated division of identical cakes between two players with private preferences. Alice chooses a cut, and Bob chooses a side. In the sequential version, Bob sees the cut before choosing; in the simultaneous version, he learns it afterward. Repetition makes each choice relevant to both the current division and what the other player can learn.

The authors show that Bob can be exploited if he chooses his immediately preferred piece too often. Alice can use a strategy resembling binary search to estimate his preferences increasingly precisely and secure a disproportionate share over time. This explains why repeatedly pursuing the best immediate outcome can create a strategic vulnerability.

The paper also establishes that players can enforce an equitable long-run utility profile of one-half each on every trajectory of play, using a connection to Blackwell approachability. Finally, it analyzes fictitious play, where each player best responds to the other's empirical behavior. This dynamic converges to the equitable profile at a rate of O(1/√T), connecting fairness guarantees with a natural adaptive strategy.
neurips-2024-dueling-over-dessert-master.tldr: Repeated cake cutting can expose myopic players to exploitation, but suitable strategies and fictitious play support equitable long-run utilities.

paragraphs: Efficient tensor operations are central to modern machine learning, but library performance depends on the workloads used to guide development. This paper identifies a mismatch in einsum libraries: they are typically tuned for expressions involving a few large, dense, floating-point tensors, while practical applications involve a much broader range of expressions.

The authors create a benchmark dataset designed to cover that broader range. Its purpose is to give future einsum implementations representative problems to build against and evaluate. This matters because strong performance on a narrow class of expressions may not translate into strong performance on the workloads users actually need to execute.

The release also includes generators for producing additional einsum expressions and converters for expressing other problems in einsum form. These tools allow the benchmark material to grow as needed. The contribution is shared evaluation infrastructure that connects execution-engine development more closely to application diversity, providing concrete workloads for assessing whether efficiency improvements extend beyond the expressions current libraries already handle well.
neurips-2024-einsum-benchmark-enabling-t.tldr: Einsum Benchmark supplies diverse tensor-expression workloads and generation tools to guide more representative execution-engine development.

paragraphs: Organizations can share pretrained molecular models without directly releasing the proprietary molecules used for training. This paper investigates whether those models can nevertheless expose training data through extraction attacks. The question matters for collaborative drug-discovery efforts that depend on sharing useful models while preserving commercial confidentiality.

Extraction is challenging because the molecular models are non-generative and vary in architecture. The authors introduce a molecule-generation approach alongside a model-independent scoring function for identifying promising candidate molecules. They also develop a Molecule Extraction Policy Network to reduce the search space efficiently. These components make candidate generation and selection central to the extraction process.

Experiments demonstrate a considerable risk of recovering training molecules even when an attacker has only query access to the pretrained model. The result challenges the assumption that withholding the training dataset while sharing the model provides adequate protection by itself. Its scope is an empirical demonstration of extraction risk through model access, with direct implications for the trust underlying molecular model-sharing initiatives.
neurips-2024-extracting-training-data-fr.tldr: A molecule-generation and selection approach demonstrates that query access to pretrained molecular models can expose private training molecules.

paragraphs: Learning-augmented algorithms use predictions to improve algorithmic decisions. Prior work has shown how accurate predictions can improve performance while worst-case guarantees provide robustness when predictions fail. For online problems, however, much of this work treats the predictor as a black box, leaving its learning process outside the algorithm's design.

This paper brings that learning process into the problem itself. The predictor can update as more of the input arrives, and its learning rule is designed for the particular algorithmic task. The central idea is to develop the decision-making algorithm and the predictor together, accounting for how prediction evolves during execution.

The authors apply this perspective to fundamental online problems, including caching and scheduling. For each problem, they introduce an algorithm paired with an explicit, carefully designed learning rule. These combinations improve overall performance compared with previous work. The contribution establishes the value of considering how predictions are learned alongside how they are used when designing online algorithms for these tasks.
neurips-2024-learning-augmented-algorith.tldr: Jointly designing online algorithms and their predictors improves performance on problems including caching and scheduling.

paragraphs: Language-model evaluations face a tension between realistic questions and efficient, dependable grading. Existing ground-truth benchmarks may poorly reflect real-world queries, while model-based judging introduces grading biases. User-facing evaluations provide useful signals but are costly and slow. MixEval aims to combine realistic query coverage with the practicality of existing benchmark answers.

The method matches queries collected from the web with similar questions from established benchmarks, then strategically mixes those benchmarks. This connects the distribution of user queries to questions with available ground-truth grading. The authors also introduce MixEval-Hard to provide more room for models to improve and a rapid, stable update pipeline to support dynamic evaluation.

The reported model-ranking correlation with Chatbot Arena is 0.96. Execution requires 6% of the time and cost of MMLU, while remaining reproducible. Extensive meta-evaluation examines both MixEval and existing benchmarks. These findings support benchmark mixing as an efficient way to approximate user-facing evaluation signals, with the reported correlation describing agreement in model rankings.
neurips-2024-mixeval-deriving-wisdom-of-.tldr: MixEval matches real-world queries to existing benchmark questions, reporting strong agreement with Chatbot Arena rankings at low evaluation cost.

paragraphs: This paper studies ReLU-network training by examining the boundaries at which individual neurons change their activation behavior. That perspective reveals a critical instability in common parameterizations and normalization approaches during stochastic optimization. The authors connect this instability to slower convergence and poorer generalization, making the representation of the weights itself a target for improvement.

Their proposed method, Geometric Parameterization, separates the radial and angular components of weights in hyperspherical coordinates. In plain terms, it treats weight magnitude and direction as distinct components of the parameterization. This geometric separation is designed to address the instability identified through the activation-boundary analysis.

The authors provide a theoretical result showing that Geometric Parameterization resolves that identified instability. They also report experiments across various models and benchmarks supporting advantages in optimization stability, convergence speed, and generalization. The contribution therefore joins an analysis of training behavior with a concrete change to network parameterization, using theory and empirical evaluation to support the proposed remedy.
neurips-2024-neural-characteristic-activ.tldr: Geometric Parameterization separates weight magnitude and direction to resolve an identified ReLU-training instability, with empirical benefits for training and generalization.

paragraphs: Decoding visual information from non-invasive brain recordings is difficult because neural signals are complex and vary between people. This paper introduces a framework that combines three-dimensional brain structure with visual meaning. Its unified feature extractor uses a Vision Transformer 3D to align fMRI features with multiple levels of visual embeddings.

The extractor supports single-trial data and removes the need for subject-specific models within the proposed framework. It consolidates multiple levels of visual features into one network, simplifying integration with large language models. The authors also enrich the fMRI dataset with varied text associated with the brain recordings and images to support multimodal model development.

The integrated system supports brain captioning, complex reasoning, concept localization, and visual reconstruction. The authors report superior performance across these tasks, including precise localization of language-based concepts in brain signals. These results connect reconstruction with language-based interpretation, broadening what the framework can extract from recordings. The contribution supports richer analysis of visual brain data and potential applications in neuroscience and human-computer interaction.
neurips-2024-neuro-vision-to-language-en.tldr: A unified 3D vision-transformer framework connects single-trial fMRI recordings to visual features and language models for reconstruction and interpretation.

paragraphs: Removing haze from real photographs is difficult because real haze distributions are complex and paired training examples are scarce. This paper addresses both the restoration model and the training supervision. Its cooperative unfolding network jointly models atmospheric scattering and image scenes, incorporating physical knowledge into a deep network to recover details obscured by haze.

To provide training targets, the authors introduce an iterative mean-teacher framework called the Coherence-based Label Generator. It produces pseudo labels and maintains a pool of the best candidates encountered during training. Both global and local coherence guide candidate selection, while weighting gives priority to haze-free regions.

The two components serve complementary purposes: the network incorporates knowledge of how haze affects images, and the label generator improves the supervision available when paired real-world data are scarce. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on real-world dehazing tasks. The stated findings support combining physically informed restoration with selective pseudo-label generation as a way to address the modeling and data challenges together.
neurips-2024-real-world-image-dehazing-w.tldr: A physically informed restoration network and coherence-based pseudo labels jointly improve real-world image dehazing.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove particular knowledge from an already trained model. RWKU creates a benchmark for evaluating this process in language models under a demanding setting: neither the corpus to forget nor the corpus to retain is accessible. It uses 200 famous people as targets and establishes that knowledge about them is widespread across various models.

The benchmark evaluates both targeted forgetting and preservation of other capabilities. Its forget set includes four membership-inference attack methods and nine kinds of adversarial probes to test unlearning efficacy. These assessments examine forgetting through multiple forms of probing, making the evaluation broader than a single way of asking about the target.

The retain set measures effects on neighboring knowledge alongside general ability, reasoning, truthfulness, factuality, and fluency. Experiments cover two unlearning scenarios, two models, and six baseline methods. The contribution is an evaluation framework that considers removal and preservation together, so unlearning can be assessed in relation to the model's remaining usefulness across real-world applications.
neurips-2024-rwku-benchmarking-real-worl.tldr: RWKU evaluates language-model unlearning without access to forget or retain corpora, testing targeted removal alongside preserved capabilities.

paragraphs: SCube reconstructs large three-dimensional scenes from a sparse collection of images with known camera poses. It represents geometry, appearance, and semantics through VoxSplats: three-dimensional Gaussians arranged on a high-resolution sparse-voxel scaffold. This combines a spatial structure for the scene with a representation of its visual appearance.

Reconstruction proceeds in two stages. An image-conditioned hierarchical latent diffusion model progressively generates the voxel grid from coarse to fine resolution. A feedforward appearance network then predicts Gaussians inside the voxels. The approach uses high-resolution sparse networks to produce sharp outputs from few views, addressing problems associated with dense view requirements and low-resolution geometric priors.

The authors report generating millions of Gaussians across scenes spanning hundreds of meters in 20 seconds from as few as three non-overlapping images. They show superior reconstruction results compared with prior work on the Waymo self-driving dataset. They also demonstrate LiDAR simulation and text-to-scene generation, showing how the reconstructed representation can support applications beyond reproducing the input images.
neurips-2024-scube-instant-large-scale-s.tldr: SCube combines hierarchical voxel diffusion with Gaussian appearance prediction to reconstruct large, sharp 3D scenes from very few posed images.

paragraphs: Instruction tuning adapts language models for interactions with people, and carefully chosen training examples can improve its effectiveness. Many data-selection approaches require additional models or data, increasing the cost of selection. SelectIT instead uses the language model's own foundational capabilities and intrinsic uncertainty to identify high-quality instruction-tuning data.

The central approach makes the model itself a resource for deciding which examples to use. The authors apply SelectIT to Alpaca-GPT4 to create a curated dataset called Selective Alpaca. This provides a concrete application of the selection method and a dataset for examining whether the selected instructions improve subsequent model abilities.

Experiments report substantial ability improvements from tuning on Selective Alpaca, with robustness supported across various foundation models and domain-specific tasks. The findings also suggest that longer instructions requiring more computation may provide better tuning material. That observation is presented as a possible direction for selecting useful data, while the main empirical contribution supports uncertainty-aware selection without additional models or data.
neurips-2024-selectit-selective-instruct.tldr: SelectIT uses a language model's own uncertainty to select instruction-tuning data, producing a curated dataset that improves evaluated model abilities.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised multi-label learning trains classifiers from a small labeled dataset and many unlabeled examples, with each example potentially having several labels. A common approach assigns pseudo labels to unlabeled data and then trains on both sources. The authors empirically identify a variance-bias problem between positive and negative feature distributions under commonly used binary losses and negative sampling.

Their method addresses this imbalance through the distribution of feature angles for each label. It extends binary angular margin loss using distribution transformations under a Gaussian assumption. The distributions are updated iteratively during training, allowing the balancing mechanism to follow the classifier's changing features.

The method also uses prototype-based negative sampling to efficiently maintain high-quality negative examples for each label. Together, these components form S²ML²-BBAM. Comparisons with existing methods on benchmark datasets show very competitive performance. The contribution ties the observed distribution imbalance to a targeted loss modification and sampling strategy, with the Gaussian assumption forming an explicit part of how the distribution transformations are constructed.
neurips-2024-semi-supervised-multi-label.tldr: S²ML²-BBAM balances positive and negative feature-angle distributions and improves negative sampling for competitive semi-supervised multi-label learning.

paragraphs: Comparing classifiers reliably involves more than choosing a single score. This paper addresses three requirements: considering multiple quality metrics, accounting for uncertainty from the benchmark suite, and checking robustness to small changes in assumptions. It develops a statistical framework that brings these requirements into the comparison process.

The framework uses generalized stochastic dominance to order classifiers and introduces the GSD-front as an information-efficient alternative to the classical Pareto-front. The authors provide a consistent estimator for this front and a statistical test for whether a classifier belongs to it. This includes assessing a potentially new classifier against a collection of state-of-the-art alternatives.

To examine robustness, the authors relax the test using tools from robust statistics and imprecise probabilities. They illustrate the framework using PMLB and OpenML. The contribution makes uncertainty and assumptions part of multicriteria benchmarking, allowing claims about competitive classifiers to be assessed statistically while retaining the fact that quality is being judged along several dimensions.
neurips-2024-statistical-multicriteria-b.tldr: The GSD-front provides a statistical framework for comparing classifiers across multiple metrics while accounting for benchmark uncertainty and assumption sensitivity.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization chooses successive evaluations to search efficiently for a good solution to a black-box problem. It commonly stops when a predefined budget runs out. This paper investigates stopping according to the probability that the search has already found a sufficiently good solution, connecting termination to solution quality.

The central criterion asks whether a solution is within a chosen tolerance, epsilon, of the optimum with probability at least one minus delta under the model. Epsilon sets the allowed gap in value, while delta sets the permitted probability of failing that condition. For Gaussian process priors, the authors show that Bayesian optimization satisfies this criterion under mild technical assumptions.

The paper also gives a practical algorithm for evaluating Monte Carlo stopping rules efficiently while accounting for estimation error. Empirical results demonstrate strengths and weaknesses of the approach. The probability statement is explicitly model-based, so the stopping rule expresses confidence under that model rather than an unconditional guarantee independent of its assumptions.
neurips-2024-stopping-bayesian-optimizat.tldr: A model-based probabilistic stopping rule lets Bayesian optimization stop when a solution is sufficiently close to optimal with specified confidence.

paragraphs: This paper studies how information travels through decoder-only Transformers. It focuses on the last token's representation in the final layer, which is used to predict the next token. The question is whether that representation preserves distinctions between inputs that may require different responses.

Through theoretical signal-propagation analysis, the authors prove that certain distinct input pairs can produce arbitrarily close final-token representations. Low-precision floating-point formats exacerbate this representational collapse. The resulting inability to respond differently to these sequences can cause errors in tasks such as counting and copying. The result concerns particular input pairs and the analyzed mechanism.

The authors also show that these models can lose sensitivity to specific input tokens, connecting the effect to information over-squashing in graph neural networks. Empirical evidence from contemporary language models supports the theoretical claims. Their theory points toward simple ways to ameliorate the problems, making the analysis useful both for explaining some failures and for identifying directions to improve information propagation.
neurips-2024-transformers-need-glasses-i.tldr: Theoretical and empirical analysis shows how decoder-only Transformers can lose input distinctions, with low precision worsening the resulting failures.

paragraphs: This paper explores whether Transformer predictions can be understood through simpler statistical rules. It constructs families of rules from N-gram statistics in the training data and measures how well they approximate the model's predictions. This provides a concrete way to study dependence on context through progressively more complex statistical templates.

The analysis yields a method for detecting overfitting during training without a holdout set and a quantitative measure of progression from simple to more complex rules. It also identifies a model-variance criterion governing when predictions tend to be described by N-gram rules. These results use approximation as a tool for studying both training behavior and prediction structure.

As the rulesets become increasingly complex, their top-ranked token agrees with the language model's top-ranked token for 79% of next-token distributions on TinyStories and 68% on Wikipedia. These figures measure agreement on the top prediction, rather than equality of entire probability distributions. The findings demonstrate substantial descriptive power for the studied rulesets while retaining that specific meaning of agreement.
neurips-2024-understanding-transformers-.tldr: N-gram rules approximate many Transformer top-token predictions and provide tools for analyzing statistical learning and detecting overfitting.
